label: Shemu'el Aleph (1 Samuel) — Part 2 — Chapters 11–17
summary_plain: Sha'ul defeats the Ammonites at Yavesh-Gil'ad and is confirmed as king. Shemu'el rebukes the people: you have asked for a king, but YHWH is your true king. Sha'ul disobeys YHWH's command against Amaleq — he spares King Agag and the best of the livestock. Shemu'el declares: to obey is better than sacrifice. YHWH rejects Sha'ul as king. YHWH sends Shemu'el to the house of Yishai in Beit-Lehem. YHWH does not look at outward appearance — he looks at the heart. Dawid, the youngest son, is anointed. The spirit of YHWH comes upon Dawid. Golyat the Philistine defies the armies of the living Creator. Dawid declares: I come to you in the name of YHWH of hosts. He strikes Golyat with a sling and a stone.
summary_scholarly: The ACR reads from 4QSam-a, 4QSam-b, and 4QSam-c alongside the Orit Ge'ez. 4QSam-a preserves a full paragraph before chapter 11 — absent from the Masoretic — describing the Ammonite king Nahash gouging out the right eyes of the men of Gad and Re'uven. This passage, confirmed by Josephus, demonstrates that the Masoretic is incomplete. Sha'ul's rejection (ch 15) establishes the covenant principle: obedience to YHWH's word supersedes all institutional ritual. Dawid's anointing (ch 16) introduces the Davidic line — YHWH's selection based on the heart, not on birth order or appearance. The Golyat narrative (ch 17) establishes victory through YHWH's name, not human military power — the same framework preserved in the Qumran War Scroll (1QM).

key_terms.definition: In 1 Shemu'el 13, before the Philistine battle at Mikhmas, Sha'ul waited seven days for Shemu'el to come and offer sacrifices. When Shemu'el did not appear and the army was scattering, Sha'ul offered the burnt offering himself — a priestly act he had no authority to perform. Shemu'el arrived immediately after and pronounced judgment: 'Your kingdom will not continue; YHWH has sought a man after his own heart.'

In 1 Shemu'el 15, YHWH commands Sha'ul to utterly destroy Amalek — people, animals, everything. Sha'ul wins the battle but spares King Agag and the best sheep and oxen. His defense: the people kept the best animals to sacrifice to YHWH. Shemu'el's response: 'Has YHWH as great delight in burnt offerings and sacrifices as in obeying the voice of YHWH? Behold, to obey is better than sacrifice; to listen than the fat of rams.'

Shemu'el's declaration to Sha'ul after the Agag disobedience (1 Shemu'el 15:22) — one of the most important covenant statements in the Torah and former prophets. Covenant fidelity is obedience, not religious performance. Sha'ul's sacrificial intention did not substitute for following YHWH's direct command. The worship system was designed to accompany obedience, not replace it.

YHWH sends Shemu'el to Bet-Lekhem to anoint a son of Yishai. Seven sons pass before Shemu'el; each time YHWH says no. The last son, David, is out in the field tending sheep. YHWH says: 'Rise and anoint him — this is he.' The key principle: 'Humans see the outward appearance, but YHWH sees the heart.'

The Philistine champion from Gat stands at over nine feet, heavily armored, and challenges Yisra'el to single combat. David, a young shepherd, volunteers. He refuses Sha'ul's armor: 'I have not tested these.' He takes his sling and five smooth stones, calls on YHWH's name, and kills Golyat with a single stone before cutting off his head with his own sword. The victory is explicitly declared as YHWH's, not David's strength.

1 Shemu'el 16:7 — YHWH's direct statement to Shemu'el when he saw Eliav and thought 'surely this is YHWH's anointed': 'Do not look at his appearance or height, for I have rejected him. Humans see the outward appearance, but YHWH sees the heart.' This principle governs all of David's selection — not birth order, not appearance, not what any human would choose.

After YHWH's spirit departed from Sha'ul, an evil spirit from YHWH tormented him. David was brought to court specifically to play the kinnor (lyre) for Sha'ul when the evil spirit came. The spirit would leave when David played. The text presents the evil spirit as YHWH's instrument — covenant absence does not leave a vacuum, but brings its own distress.

1 Shemu'el 17:45-47: 'You come against me with sword, spear, and javelin, but I come against you in the name of YHWH of Hosts, the Creator of the armies of Yisra'el, whom you have defied. This day YHWH will deliver you into my hand... that all the earth may know there is a Creator in Yisra'el... for the battle is YHWH's, and he will give you into our hand.'

David's father, an Efratite of Bet-Lekhem in the tribe of Yehudah. He had eight sons; David was the youngest. Yishai's lineage connects back through Ovet to Rut the Moavite and Boaz — the same covenant family line that preserved covenant faithfulness in the dark days between the judges. David's roots in Bet-Lekhem and in Yehudah are established here.

The strategic pass where the Philistines camped in 1 Shemu'el 13-14. Sha'ul's son Yehonatan and his armor-bearer crossed to the Philistine garrison alone, declaring: 'Nothing can hinder YHWH from saving, whether by many or by few.' YHWH sent an earthquake that caused confusion among the Philistines. Yehonatan's initiative routed the camp before Sha'ul even engaged.

faq.question: What does 'a man after YHWH's own heart' mean for David?
faq.answer: The phrase is YHWH's own designation, not human praise. It appears first in Shemu'el's condemnation of Sha'ul: 'YHWH has sought a man after his own heart.' It does not mean a perfect man — David's later adultery and murder place him far from moral perfection. It means a man whose fundamental orientation is toward YHWH: who returns to YHWH after failure, whose laments and praises are covenant speech, who does not abandon covenant loyalty even when it costs him politically. The heart in covenant theology is not emotions but the seat of will and direction. David's heart is set toward YHWH even when his actions betray YHWH.

faq.question: Why was Sha'ul's sacrifice at Mikhmas disqualifying?
faq.answer: Sha'ul was not a priest. The covenant structure established at Sinai separated the roles of king, priest, and prophet. Sha'ul's unauthorized sacrifice was not primarily a matter of impatience — it was a category violation, mixing covenant roles that were specifically separated. His defense ('I forced myself and offered') is precisely the problem: a king who forces covenant structure to fit his military situation has placed his own authority above YHWH's design. Shemu'el's response is immediate: the kingdom will not continue in his family. The first disobedience was not a minor incident but a character revelation.

faq.question: What does the Golyat story say about YHWH's military theology?
faq.answer: David's declaration before the battle is the theological core: 'You come with sword, spear, and javelin — I come in the name of YHWH of Hosts.' Military equipment against covenant name. The battle's outcome demonstrates which is greater. David explicitly says the purpose of the victory is testimony: 'that all the earth may know there is a Creator in Yisra'el.' Covenant military victories are never purely strategic — they are declarations of YHWH's reality to the nations. The battle belongs to YHWH; human participants are instruments, not architects, of the outcome.

faq.question: What does Sha'ul's response to the Agag command reveal?
faq.answer: Sha'ul's defense — 'the people took the best animals to sacrifice to YHWH at Gilgal' — is the classic pattern of using covenant worship as cover for disobedience. He did not disobey by abandoning worship; he disobeyed by substituting his own interpretation of how to honor YHWH for YHWH's direct instruction. Shemu'el's response cuts to the theological core: worship is not a currency that pays for selective obedience. YHWH does not want the sacrifice of animals that should have been destroyed in obedience to his command; he wants the obedience that makes such sacrifice unnecessary. The worship system presupposes obedience; it does not replace it.

faq.question: Why was David's youngest-son status significant?
faq.answer: In covenant pattern, the youngest, least expected choice is consistent: Hevel over Qayin, Yitzhak over Yishmael, Ya'akov over Esav, Yehudah and Yosef over Reuven, Efrayim over Menasheh. David follows the pattern: eight sons presented, the youngest not even thought worth calling in from the field. His father Yishai brought seven sons before Shemu'el without mentioning David. YHWH's choice always subverts human birth-order logic. The covenant line runs through the unexpected, the marginal, the overlooked — which is consistent with YHWH's character as the one who lifts the poor from the dust.

faq.question: What is the significance of David refusing Sha'ul's armor?
faq.answer: Sha'ul dressed David in his own coat of mail, bronze helmet, and sword. David tried them and said: 'I cannot go with these because I have not tested them.' He took them off and went with his staff, sling, and five smooth stones. The armor refusal is not false modesty — it is covenant strategy. David's strength against Golyat was YHWH's name, not Sha'ul's equipment. Fighting in Sha'ul's armor would have meant fighting on the same terms as Golyat — military equipment against military equipment. David's instrument (a sling) was what YHWH could work through. The covenant victory required covenant weapons, not borrowed military dress.

faq.question: What does the evil spirit sent to Sha'ul mean theologically?
faq.answer: The text states explicitly: an evil spirit 'from YHWH' tormented Sha'ul. This is a difficult statement. The covenant framework in the former prophets holds YHWH responsible for all outcomes in Yisra'el's history — including destructive spirits. When YHWH's spirit departed from Sha'ul, the resulting distress was not random; it was the experience of covenant absence. The evil spirit is not an independent demonic force opposed to YHWH — it is under YHWH's authority and sent by him. The theological claim: when YHWH withdraws covenant presence, what fills the space is not neutral. The same Creator who gives peace also sends the distress that accompanies covenant departure.

faq.question: What is the significance of Yehonatan's raid at Mikhmas?
faq.answer: Yehonatan's declaration — 'nothing can hinder YHWH from saving, whether by many or by few' — and his subsequent raid with only his armor-bearer demonstrates covenant faith in action. He did not wait for the army's permission; he acted on his own conviction about YHWH's willingness to save. YHWH responded with an earthquake that caused confusion in the Philistine camp. The raid is the counterpoint to Sha'ul's unauthorized sacrifice: Yehonatan acted without authority in a militarily reckless way, and YHWH honored it because his heart was entirely covenant-focused. Yehonatan's character — faithful, without political ambition, genuinely oriented toward YHWH — is established here as the foil to both his father and later events.

faq.question: What does 'YHWH sees the heart' mean in the anointing context?
faq.answer: The statement is made when Shemu'el sees Eliav and assumes he must be the anointed one. YHWH says: 'Do not look at his appearance or height — I have rejected him. Humans see the outward appearance; YHWH sees the heart.' This is not a prohibition on appearance mattering at all — Sha'ul's impressive appearance was part of his selection, and David himself is described as handsome. The principle is about priority: YHWH's selection criterion is interior, not exterior. The heart (will, direction, covenant orientation) is what YHWH is looking at. This principle governs YHWH's covenant choices throughout — it is the same logic as YHWH choosing Yisra'el: not because they were greatest but because YHWH loved them and kept his oath.

faq.question: How does David's Bet-Lekhem lineage connect to the broader covenant narrative?
faq.answer: David is from Bet-Lekhem in Yehudah. His grandfather was Ovet, the son of Rut (the Moavite) and Boaz. The Book of Rut is set explicitly 'in the days when the judges judged' — the dark period of Shofetim. While all Yisra'el was cycling through covenant failure, a Moavite woman's covenant loyalty to Naomi, her declaration 'your people shall be my people and your Creator my Creator,' placed her in the direct ancestral line of David. YHWH's covenant line runs through faithful choices by individuals even in the worst historical moments. David's lineage includes a foreign woman whose loyalty to Naomi was itself covenant faithfulness.
